erhebung-0.bring: Nothing personal: an invented interview excerpt of about 200 words, written by you or generated by Copilot in step 1.
steps: Ask Copilot to invent a 200-word two-person interview excerpt on your topic, without speaker labels.
Paste the starter prompt with that excerpt and choose a target language you can read.
Compare the labelled version line by line with the original excerpt.
Note where it changed wording, merged speakers or smoothed over hesitations.
erhebung-0.prompt: Below is a short, invented interview excerpt between an interviewer and one participant, with no speaker labels. 1) Add labels (I: and P:) at each change of speaker, keeping the wording exactly as it is. 2) Mark any place where the speaker is unclear with [unclear]. 3) Translate the labelled text into [language], keeping hesitations and repetitions. Show the original and the translation side by side in a two-column table. Do not summarise, shorten or correct the speakers' grammar. Excerpt: [paste invented text]
erhebung-0.check: Every sentence of the original appears unchanged in the labelled version and the translation keeps the meaning; real interviews must only go through your university's approved transcription tool, never into this chat.
erhebung-0.limit: Copilot Chat cannot transcribe audio files, so this tests only speaker labelling and translation of an invented text excerpt.

erhebung-1.bring: An open-access PDF with figures or tables, such as an annual report, a government statistics release or an open-access paper.
steps: Attach the PDF, or only the relevant pages of a long report.
Paste the starter prompt with the fields you want extracted.
Spot-check five values against the PDF using the cited page numbers.
Copy the checked table into Excel or ask Copilot for a CSV file.
erhebung-1.prompt: I am collecting data from documents for a research project on [topic]. From the attached PDF, extract these fields: [field 1, field 2, field 3, e.g. year, revenue, number of staff, stated goals]. Return a table with one row per [unit, e.g. year or organisation] and a column for each field, plus the page number and a short verbatim quote as evidence for each value. If a value is missing or ambiguous, write 'not found' rather than estimating. Do not use any information from outside the document.
erhebung-1.check: Five randomly chosen values match the PDF exactly on the cited page, and 'not found' appears only where the document really lacks the value.

erhebung-2.bring: Your coding scheme (3–6 codes with definitions) and 20 short non-sensitive texts, such as open-access abstracts or invented statements, numbered in a list or CSV.
steps: Code ten of the texts yourself before opening Copilot and keep your codes aside.
Paste the starter prompt with your scheme and all texts, or attach the CSV.
Paste your own ten codes and ask Copilot to calculate Cohen's kappa in Python.
Read every disagreement and decide whether the scheme or Copilot was unclear.
erhebung-2.prompt: I am testing whether a language model can pre-annotate texts for my study on [topic]. Coding scheme: [code: definition, one per line]. Assign exactly one code to each text below (or in the attached file). Return a table: text ID, code, confidence (high, medium or low), and a one-sentence reason that quotes the text. Use 'unclear' if no code fits; do not create new codes. Texts: [paste numbered texts]
erhebung-2.check: Agreement of roughly 0.6 kappa or above, with disagreements you can explain, suggests the scheme is ready for a larger test; lower agreement means refining the code definitions first.
erhebung-2.limit: Copilot Chat lets you test the scheme on a small sample; pre-annotating large volumes needs a scripted pipeline in an approved tool.

erhebung-3.bring: Three draft interview or survey questions on a non-sensitive topic from your research.
steps: Paste the starter prompt with your three core questions.
Answer as an invented respondent, including one vague and one off-topic answer.
After the last question, read Copilot's list of follow-ups and reasons.
Check each follow-up for leading wording, pressure or drift outside your topic.
erhebung-3.prompt: I am designing an adaptive interview on [topic] for [population] and want to pilot it. Act as the interviewer. Ask my core questions one at a time: [Q1], [Q2], [Q3]. After each answer, ask at most one neutral follow-up to clarify or deepen it. Rules: no leading questions, no questions about health, finances or other sensitive matters, accept 'I'd rather not say' without pushing, and stay within the topic. I will answer as an invented respondent. After the last question, list each follow-up you asked and your reason for it.
erhebung-3.check: Each follow-up is neutral, tied to the answer just given and within your topic; a real study needs ethics approval, informed consent and an approved platform before any participant talks to an AI interviewer.
erhebung-3.limit: Copilot Chat cannot run a survey with participants; this tests drafting and piloting adaptive follow-ups, with you playing an invented respondent.

erhebung-4.bring: Your research question and a note of the data you need: country, time period, unit of analysis and key variables.
steps: Paste the starter prompt with your research question and data requirements.
Open each suggested link and check coverage, access conditions and latest update.
Remove any dataset you cannot find or that lacks your key variables.
Ask Copilot to rank the confirmed datasets by fit to your question.
erhebung-4.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher in [discipline]. My research question is: [question]. I need secondary data covering [country or region] and [time period], at the level of [individuals, firms, regions or texts], with variables on [key variables]. Search the web for open datasets and repositories (for example the UK Data Service, national statistics offices, Zenodo or discipline repositories). Give up to six options as a table: name, provider, link, coverage, access conditions, fit and what is missing. If you are not sure a dataset includes a variable, say so; do not invent datasets.
erhebung-4.check: Each link leads to a real dataset page whose documentation confirms the coverage and at least one key variable Copilot claimed.

erhebung-5.bring: Nothing real: an invented interview excerpt of about 200 words containing made-up names, places, employers and dates.
steps: Write, or ask Copilot to invent, a 200-word excerpt with fictional names, places and dates.
Note every identifier you planted, including indirect ones such as a rare job title.
Paste the starter prompt with the excerpt.
Compare the output with your list and mark every identifier missed or not flagged.
erhebung-5.prompt: Below is an invented interview excerpt. Pseudonymise it for qualitative analysis. Replace personal names with [P1], [P2]; places with [CITY] or [REGION]; organisations with [ORG1], [ORG2]; exact dates with [DATE]; and keep everything else word for word. Also flag, without changing them, indirect identifiers that could reveal someone in combination, such as rare job titles or distinctive events. Return 1) the pseudonymised text and 2) a table: original term, replacement, type. Excerpt: [paste invented text]
erhebung-5.check: Search the output for each identifier you planted; any that remain or go unflagged show why real transcripts need an approved environment and a full manual check.
erhebung-5.limit: This tests the method on an invented excerpt only; never paste real transcripts or participants' data into Copilot Chat.

erhebung-6.bring: A photo or scan of one page of public-domain printed or handwritten material, ideally from a digitised archive that also offers a transcription.
steps: Attach the image of a single page or a short section.
Paste the starter prompt with the language and approximate date.
Compare five lines with the archive's transcription or your own careful reading.
Ask for a draft translation of the lines you have confirmed only.
erhebung-6.prompt: I am a researcher working with archival sources. The attached image shows a [printed or handwritten] document in [language], from around [date or period]. Transcribe it line by line, keeping the original spelling, abbreviations and line breaks. Mark uncertain readings with [?] and illegible parts with [illegible] rather than guessing. Then give a literal draft translation into modern English, line by line, in a two-column table. Note any words whose meaning may have changed since that period.
erhebung-6.check: In five lines checked against the existing transcription or the image, every word not marked [?] is correct; if you find confident errors, treat the whole output as a rough draft.
erhebung-6.limit: Copilot Chat works page by page; transcribing whole collections needs dedicated OCR or handwriting recognition tools.

analyse-0.bring: A public or dummy dataset as CSV and an analysis you want to run, or a short analysis script of your own that throws an error.
steps: Attach the CSV and describe the analysis, naming your software.
Ask for commented code plus a plain explanation of each step.
For Python, ask Copilot to run it; otherwise run it in your own software.
Paste any error message back and ask for a fix with an explanation.
analyse-0.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher in [discipline] using [R, Python, Stata or SPSS]. The attached file is a [public or dummy] dataset with the variables [key variables]. I want to [analysis, e.g. run a linear regression of Y on X1 and X2 with robust standard errors]. Write commented code that loads the data, checks variable types and missing values, runs the analysis and prints the results. Then explain in plain language what each block does and which assumptions I should check. If a function or option may not exist in my version, say so.
analyse-0.check: The code runs without errors and one key number, such as the sample size or a mean, matches what you get by checking the data directly.
analyse-0.limit: Copilot runs Python only; code in R, Stata or SPSS has to be run and checked in your own software.

analyse-1.bring: A small public or dummy CSV or Excel file with some messy values, such as misspelt categories, blanks or implausible numbers.
steps: Attach the file and paste the starter prompt.
Review the issue table and decide which fixes you accept.
Ask Copilot to apply only those fixes and show the Python script.
Ask for the cleaned file and a log of every change made.
analyse-1.prompt: I am preparing a dataset for analysis. The attached file contains [public or dummy data on topic]; each row is a [unit]. Use Python to profile it: missing values per column, inconsistent category spellings, duplicate rows, and out-of-range or implausible values (valid ranges: [e.g. age 18–99]). Report the issues as a table: column, problem, number of rows, example values, suggested fix. Do not change the data yet. Show the code you used so I can rerun it later.
analyse-1.check: Confirm two or three of the reported problems by hand in the original file, then check the cleaned file has the row count you expect.

analyse-2.bring: Two or three short invented interview excerpts, or quotes from an open-access qualitative paper, and your research question; never your participants' data.
steps: Paste the starter prompt with your research question and the excerpts.
Check that each code has a clear definition and a fitting example quote.
Compare the coding with your own first reading of the excerpts.
Note what Copilot missed, flattened or over-interpreted.
analyse-2.prompt: I am a qualitative researcher in [discipline]. My research question is: [question]. Below are [number] short excerpts for practice. Propose a coding frame of 5–8 codes, each with a one-line definition and an example quote. Then code each excerpt, showing the exact passage for every code applied. Finally, suggest how the codes might group into 2–3 broader categories, and point out where an excerpt could be read in more than one way. Do not go beyond what the text says. Excerpts: [paste text]
analyse-2.check: Every quoted passage appears word for word in the excerpts and you can name at least one code you would define differently; in reflexive approaches, treat the output as a prompt for your own thinking, not as coding.

analyse-3.bring: A CSV of 50–200 short public texts, such as open-access abstracts or public product reviews with author names removed, plus an ID column.
steps: Attach the CSV and paste the starter prompt, naming the text column.
Read ten of the labelled texts yourself and count how many you agree with.
Read two texts from each topic and judge whether the top words fit.
Ask Copilot to change the number of topics and compare the results.
analyse-3.prompt: I am exploring text as data for a project on [topic]. The attached CSV has [number] texts in the column [column name]. 1) For the first 30 rows, assign a sentiment (positive, neutral or negative) or one of these categories: [categories with definitions], with a one-line reason. 2) Using Python, run a simple topic model on all rows with [5] topics and show the top ten words per topic and the code. State the method and settings used, and say where results look unstable.
analyse-3.check: You agree with at least eight of the ten labels you check by hand, and the topics still look similar when the number of topics changes slightly.
analyse-3.limit: Copilot Chat can test this on a small sample; classifying a large corpus with a language model needs a scripted pipeline outside the chat.

analyse-4.bring: A public dataset as CSV or Excel that you already know a little about, such as an ONS table or a file from a data repository.
steps: Attach the file and paste the starter prompt with two plain-language questions.
Ask Copilot to show the Python code behind every number it reports.
Ask a follow-up question about any pattern that surprises you.
Verify one result yourself in Excel or your usual software.
analyse-4.prompt: I am exploring a dataset before formal analysis. The attached file contains [description: source, unit, period]. First describe its structure: number of rows and columns, variable types and missing values. Then answer: [question 1, e.g. How is income distributed?] and [question 2, e.g. Does X differ between groups of Y?]. For each answer give a summary table or chart, the Python code used, and one sentence of caution, for example about outliers or small groups. Treat all findings as exploratory, not confirmed.
analyse-4.check: The row count and one summary statistic match what you get by opening the file in Excel, and any pattern Copilot reports is visible in its chart.

analyse-5.bring: A small public or dummy dataset as CSV or Excel and a rough idea of the message the figure should show.
steps: Attach the data and paste the starter prompt with your message and audience.
Choose one of the suggested chart types and ask Copilot to draw it.
Ask for changes to labels, colours or size to meet your journal's figure guidelines.
Save the final Python code alongside your data.
analyse-5.prompt: I need a publication-quality figure for a [journal article or thesis chapter] in [discipline]. The attached file contains [variables]. The figure should show [message, e.g. how X changed over time by group]. Suggest two or three suitable chart types with one line on each. Then create the best one in Python (matplotlib), with clear axis labels including units, a colour-blind-safe palette, no unnecessary decoration, and a size of [e.g. 17 cm wide] at 300 dpi. Show the full code so I can reproduce it.
analyse-5.check: Two or three plotted values match the data, and the figure stays readable in greyscale and at its printed size.

analyse-6.bring: 50–150 lines of your own non-confidential code, without passwords, API keys or data, or a short description of a small model you want to build.
steps: Paste the starter prompt with your code, naming the language and purpose.
Read the explanation and check it matches what you intended the code to do.
Ask for unit tests for one function if they were not included.
Run the tests in your own environment, or in Copilot if the code is Python.
analyse-6.prompt: I am a researcher writing [language] code for [purpose, e.g. an agent-based simulation of X]. Below is part of my own code. Please 1) explain what it does in plain language, 2) list possible bugs, edge cases and numerical issues, 3) suggest a refactored version with clear names and docstrings that keeps the behaviour the same, and 4) write unit tests in [pytest or testthat] covering normal and edge cases. If you are unsure about the intended behaviour, ask rather than assume. Code: [paste code]
analyse-6.check: The tests run, the refactored version gives the same output as your original on the same input, and you can reproduce each bug it reports.

publikation-0.bring: The abstract and section headings, or a one- to two-page extended outline, of your own paper or chapter, and the name of a target journal.
steps: Paste the starter prompt with your outline and target journal.
Compare the three-sentence summary with what you mean to argue.
Ask for one concrete fix for the weakest step in the argument.
Check the suggested structure against the journal's author guidelines.
publikation-0.prompt: I am writing a [paper or thesis chapter] in [discipline] for [target journal]. Below is my [abstract and outline]. 1) Summarise my central argument in three sentences. 2) Map the line of argument step by step and mark where a step is missing, assumed or not supported by the evidence described. 3) Suggest changes to the structure to fit a typical [article type, e.g. empirical IMRaD] article in this journal. Be specific and refer to my section headings. Do not rewrite my text. Text: [paste text]
publikation-0.check: The three-sentence summary matches what you intend to argue; where it does not, the gap shows you where your text is unclear.

publikation-1.bring: One or two paragraphs (up to 300 words) of your own writing; not a co-author's text without their consent.
steps: Paste the starter prompt with your paragraph, discipline and readership.
Go through the change table and accept or reject each edit.
Rewrite any sentence where the edit no longer sounds like you.
Check your university's rules on proofreading before using this on a thesis.
publikation-1.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher in [discipline] writing in English as my [first or second] language, for [readership, e.g. a journal in my field]. Edit the paragraph below for clarity, precision and flow in UK English, keeping my meaning, terminology and citations unchanged. Do not add new content or claims. Return 1) the edited paragraph and 2) a table: original phrase, change, reason. Mark any sentence where my meaning is unclear instead of guessing. Paragraph: [paste text]
publikation-1.check: Read both versions side by side: no technical term, number, hedge or citation has changed, and you understand and agree with every change in the table.

publikation-2.bring: A short paper or draft section of your own, as Word or PDF, with an abstract, at least one table and a reference list.
steps: Attach the document and paste the starter prompt.
Check each flagged item in the document yourself before changing anything.
Change one number in your copy on purpose and attach it again.
See whether a rerun of the prompt catches the planted mismatch.
publikation-2.prompt: I am checking my own [paper or chapter] before submission. In the attached document, check consistency: 1) numbers (sample sizes, percentages, statistics) that differ between the abstract, main text and tables; 2) key terms or abbreviations used inconsistently; 3) in-text citations missing from the reference list, and references never cited. Return a table: issue type, location (section or page), what each place says, suggested fix. Only report what you find in the document; if parts were too long to read fully, say which.
publikation-2.check: At least three flagged issues are real when you look them up, and the planted mismatch is caught; if not, check long documents section by section.
